March 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
Theme of the month: It takes a village to run a
Guild. Please get involved.
I was most impressed by the diversity of last
month’s response to the President’s Challenge.
Generally my intent is to pitch each challenge so
that people have a little bit of latitude as to how
they interpret the challenge – well done everyone!
The President’s Challenge for April is “texture”. Yes
I know we had embellishment a while back, but
embellishment and texture are not necessarily the
same…
A massive thank you is extended to Ted Muir for
providing very relevant and important content for
our newsletter. His installments on safety, in the
past couple of editions, are also being adopted as
permanent fixtures on our website. Great stuff
Ted!! Speaking of the Newsletter a shout out to Diana Dougherty for scoping out the Member Profiles. These are a must read for me each month.
And of course tip your hat to our long suffering
(apologies Stuart McLean) Newsletter editor Steve
Fairbairn. He loves articles to inject into our already
awesome newsletter.
Sawdust huddle anyone? This is an invite to anyone
within the Guild that has an idea for a sawdust huddle. What is a sawdust huddle you may ask? It is an
informal meetup of people to turn some wood,
maybe with a theme, or particular focus. We have
access to the KMS Workshop pretty much anytime
we want for hosting one. All it takes is for someone
(that would be YOU) to make it happen – send an
email to the president@gvwg.ca to kick-start your
huddle.
Galleries! We love gallery items brought to the
meeting. We have two galleries. The Instant Gallery
which is open to any turning you have ever made,
no matter when you made it and/or any jig or tool
or other implement to share with the group. Then
there’s the President’s Challenge, the monthly task
of responding to the challenge. It’s a competition of
sorts, but only between you and your willingness to
accept it.
As for the theme of the month, I am serious. Membership begins with paying dues but is really only
vested when you contribute some time and sweat
to the Guild. Everyone has something to give back
in some way. Getting involved has its rewards.
Steve

This little 5” x 9” nugget was a
road find off our road at Harrison East. BC Hydro line clearing
crews regularly attend to the
overgrowth and leave us locals
to scramble over little piles of
free firewood. Of course we
don’t see this as firewood do
we. I roughly green turned it,
sealed it and left it to dry in the
shop for about a year. It was returned and hollowed with the ”
Simple Hollowing System ” articulating tool. The two borders
were cut out and burnt in with a
copper wire. The carving, which
was inspired by a class with Elizabeth Weber, was done with a
Dremel 4300 and flame burr. I
painted and dry brushed the piece
with many different colours but
never cared much for the look.
Finally it was repainted all black,
the raised areas dry brushed with
dark blue and again with the silver
then completed with a coat of lacquer.

A couple of years ago I pulled the trigger on a
Sundstrom
air
supplied
respirator.
Between
woodturning and my past profession as a firefighter I figured I had pushed my luck about as far as I
dared. I love it and should have done it sooner. The
down side is that it cost more than some folks
would dare to spend on a lathe.
Not long ago, while rambling through Amazon, I
spotted something that seemed too good to be
true: A supplied air respirator for $150!!! Reading
the text it’s clearly oriented for organic vapours but
it has filters and filters are often interchangeable.
The big thing about a supplied air respirator is not
just that it supplies filtered air. It also provides positive pressure inside the mask, so keeping the bad
stuff out that’s at atmospheric pressure. Most have
a filter/pump unit behind the operator, but this
one is in front, so that might be a bit of a bother,
but for about 10% or less of the cost of most powered respirators, that might be worth dealing with.
There is also no particular rating on the face shield
itself (although it appears that it might be suitable)
but then it’s also held against the head by a full
webbing, so unlikely to be knocked off as is possible with most shields.
I asked Brian to bring it up at the Tech Talk meeting
or just the regular chat, but I also posted it on the
Canadian Woodturners FB page. One fellow decided to take a chance and buy one. Here are his
thoughts.
I just received my order and I am very pleased
with the quality and manufacturing. The instructions are only in Chinese but the assembly is
straightforward. Charging it up now. Looking to
use it in my epoxy and painting.
An update on this mask. I’ve used it in both dusty
and epoxy environments. Excellent fit and comfort. Two speed air flow available and I found
the lower speed quite adequate. Flow removes
the moisture that usually builds up on static
masks. Screen is full and crystal clear. Only detractors I experienced were the belt is shorter
than my girth and the flexibility of the hose from
the air pump. Quiet and lightweight. Recharges
quickly although it lasted through the periods
(30 minutes plus) I used it. Very happy with my
purchase.
This is the link on the Amazon page. For $150 I
think it’s worth a serious look. By comparison, a full
face (non powered) respirator is usually in the
neighbourhood of $250.
I’m pretty sure one could figure out a way to manage the flex hose, perhaps over the shoulder or on
the side. I’m also pretty sure if the filter wasn’t adequate for wood dust, another could be adapted.

Tired of filing the dents out of your tool rest from
catches ?
How to convert your tool rest from a soft, dented
surface to a case hardened absolutely smooth
chrome plated steel surface?
Ed Pretty first explained to me how easy it was to
accomplish and gave me details, links and confidence to proceed with this project.
It’s easy!
Buy some 8mm dia. Case Hardened Steel Rod. You
can get it at Amazon, or locally. Lots of it around
now because it is used in 3D printers. Cut it in
lengths with an abrasive wheel like a side grinder
to run the length of your tool rest. Some add a ¼”
extra on each end. You will need to use the grinder
to “Sand” the rough cut edges of the rod to avoid
cuts to your fingers. You can also score the rod all
the way around with a grinder then snap the piece
off and grind the remaining edge smooth.
Also buy JB Weld “Cold Weld” 24 hour cure epoxy.
It’s important that you buy the right stuff. Available
at Lordco, Canadian Tire, Home Depot etc.
Now you are ready:
Do a final last filing on the
surface of your cast tool rest
to get a flat surface. Do not
sand or wax it. You want a
surface that the epoxy can
grip.
Next lay your tool rest on a flat
surface with some flat sticks,
tongue depressors or oversized
tooth picks to raise your tool rest
off the flat surface evenly and use
painters tape to snugly fit the 8mm
rod against the tool rest.
Next make a small batch of
epoxy and put a small
amount on two or three
places like a “tack weld” to
create a bond between the
rod and tool rest. Leave it
for at least 4 hours. I would
recommend a full day.
Now you can remove the holding tape and see the
rod is now fixed; tack welded” to the tool rest.
Next you use more
painters
tape
to
create a nice glue
line half way on the
rod making sure the
rod has no epoxy
on the surface that
your bowl gouge
will be gliding on.
Put painters tape on the tool rest.
Now make a bigger batch of epoxy and basically
caulk the whole line making sure you get the epoxy
deep into the cracks to eliminate any voids. You
could do the one side and let cure for 4 hours so
(Continued on page 7)

Page 7
the epoxy does not sag
from where you placed it,
then flip the rest over
and fill the other side.
Ed did both sides at the
same time after the “tack
welding”
Or just do one side one
day and the other the next day.
Let this all cure for 24 hours before using.
Smooth out the epoxy with gloved hands using methyl hydrate if you wish but it is not necessary. Just
makes it look good.
You can watch this whole process on this YouTube
video from D-Way Tools in Washington State.
Link below:
D-Way Tool Rest Top Bar Upgrade (youtube.com)
or
D-Way Tool Rest Top Bar Upgrade - YouTube
A great suggestion from Ed Pretty: “I would caution folks to make sure their present rest can sit low
enough that the additional height of the rod won’t
cause a problem with getting the rest as low as
they might want in the future. Probably not an issue normally, but I purchased rod thicker than I
had planned to get the right lengths I needed and
am now able to get it as low as I need but on occasion, just barely. If a rest is thick enough that this
might be a problem, it’s a simple matter to grind
the top low enough prior to adding the rod.”
I made the mistake of grinding the rod slightly on
one side so that the JB Weld had something to
grab. Great idea but sloppy work. I had one area
that was right where the tool would run. I was able
to use diamond bench stones to remove the grinding marks very successfully. I used 600, 1200 and
6000 grits successively and the rod is as shiny and
smooth as original. So, if there is damage to a rod,
it is possible to repair it.
I can’t remember ever dropping a rest – ever – but
I dropped one the other day. The rod popped off
but it was no problem to take the JB Weld off with
a wire wheel then reattach it again.
Note on Case Hardening: It’s a process used to
strengthen metal by introducing special elements
like carbon that increase the hardness on the surface while maintaining the flexibility and strength
of the core material.
To understand the advantage of case hardening
over normally hardened steel…
D-Way sells their normally hardened rod for tools
which is about Rockwell 62-65, so basically only as
hard as the tools that will ride on the rest. Case
hardening or surface hardening is the process of
hardening the surface of a metal object while allowing the metal deeper underneath to remain
softer (but still very hard), thus forming a thin layer
of harder metal at the surface. This is done in a variety of ways, but the more common method is to
flame harden the piece after initial hardening. A
good example of case hardening that most folks
are familiar with is roller or ball bearings. The races
and balls/rollers are case hardened to resist surface wear while the body of the steel is not as
hard, therefore much tougher and able to withstand impact and constant load. Case hardened rod
can’t be bent, so that would mean that the curved
rests that Robust sells are only hardened rod, not
case hardened, which is evident in the cleverly
worded description.

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
When my children were little and in daycare, they
learned a clean-up song. The lyrics were “Clean up,
clean up everybody, everywhere. Clean up, clean
up everybody do their share.”
One of the great things about being a GVWG member is the wood list emails alerting members to
wood that is available. Sometimes it’s a city tree on
the side of the road sometimes it someone who is
removing a tree from their property and would like
to see the wood used for something other than
woodchips. Recently I went to pick up some wood
that I heard about from one of the guilds emails.
Upon arriving I knew another wood collector had
already been there and they had left a mess. I have
no idea if they were a guild member or just another woodturner, but I am confident they were a
woodturner. How do I know? Well, there were
wood shavings on the grass and sidewalk from
chainsaw use. But the giveaway that a woodturner
was there was the thin slabs of wood with a layer
of bark on them and the 2-3” thick cookies that
were scattered around the grass. Having picked up
lots of wood from downed city trees I know the city
workers rake up after themselves and leave the
area very clean. In this recent wood pick, within 5
minutes of my chainsaw starting up someone came
out from the house I was in front of and said “I
sure hope you’re going to clean up this mess”. He
was not happy. I apologized for the mess someone
else left behind and assured him I would leave the
place nice and clean.
We are very fortunate to be able to collect wood
from city trees and I hope that when we do, we
clean up after ourselves and don’t leave a mess of
shavings and off cuts for a homeowner to clean up.
When I head out on a wood collection outing, not
only do I take my chainsaw, but a rake, broom and
a couple of garbage bags go into the car as well.
When I’m finished loading the wood, I sweep the
sidewalk and road, rake up the shavings and load
them into my garbage bags to take home with me.
I then collect the wood off-cuts and pile them neatly up against any remaining logs I’m not taking. My
goal is to leave the area clean and not make any
work for a homeowner who already has a downed
tree lying in front of their home. So, next time you
head out to collect some wood, I hope you do your
share and clean up.

March 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
I grew up in a “woody” family. My grandfather was
a mason. My father was a general contractor. My
mother was a competent woodworker. My brother was consummate handyman. You would think it
was in my genes but no such luck. I’ve always been
a bit of hacker. My first job was pulling nails on job
sites and later was turned down by the Navy on an
application to be a shipwright. I suspected that
they had seen some my work but they said because I had a degree, I had to be an officer. So for
the next 30 years, I changed naval jobs every 3
years (it’s just the way Navy does things). The upside is that I spent a lot of my career learning new
skills. I’ve been retired about 20 years now.
Tell us about your workshop/studio
My workshop is in the “crawl space” in my
house. The good news is that it’s about 300 sq/
ft. The bad news is that the ceiling is about
6’ ( used to be 6’ 2” but I'm shrinking fast: that
means I only skim my head occasionally). I have
most of my “flat work” tools (planer, drum sander,
table saw etc.) on rollers and they are pushed into
the corners. The lathes, bandsaw, drill press and
portable tools are out and used more often. I have
a 1 1/2 hp dust extractor and more importantly a
large squirrel fan with outside discharge. I keep my
air compressor and metal tools in another section
of the crawl space. That way the bench vice, welder and grinders (2) produce their sparks at a distance from my sawdust.
My “Studio” is upstairs in my living quarters. The
house is located on Marine Drive in White Rock so
I’m able to tap into the foot traffic. That being
said, I only put out my sign when I feel like it. However, it does mean that I have to keep my living
space reasonably clean.
(Continued on page 10)
Workshop
Studio

March 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
Years ago, Dan Breck and Rich Schmid talked me
into upgrading my midi lathe to a used Oneway
2436. Best advice I’ve had. My favourite gouge is
a 5/8” bowl with a finger nail grind. I have several
of these so I rarely have to interrupt my focus to
sharpen. I, like most of us, have a fair collection of
other gouges but none that are used as much as
the 5/8’s. Then, there is my growing collection of
hollowing tools. I started out making hand held
goose neck tools but found my skill at using off
centre gouges is marginal at best. I purchased an
Elbo system from Tim Yoder and found that to be
an excellent system. It’s use of the tailstock for
support and laser set up showed me that hollowing
doesn’t have to be nerve racking. I could easily
make 8” pieces with thin walls. But you know how
it goes; I wanted to go bigger. Phil Vetra sold me a
“Lyle Jamieson” style captured system. Again, a
very good way to make those 15” deep vases with
a reduced risk of catches. At this point, I needed a
steady rest, so I made one out of plywood. Maybe
it was my design or construction but it just wasn’t
strong enough for the big cherry spittoons I was
making. I borrowed two Oneway bowl rests and
although
they
worked,
I
don’t
like
to
“permanently” borrow things. I looked at commercially available set ups but they were beyond what
I was willing to spend. I designed and built my
steady
rest
with
my
non-existent
welding
skills. Likewise, I built a 5’ boring bar from some 1
1/2” bar. Although I haven’t done so yet, my plan
is to do some 30’’ vases.
What is your favourite wood?
I really don’t have a “favourite” wood. I’m fortunate to have some GVWG buddies who occasionally come across downed trees. We have a day of it
and all go home with a good supply. I enjoy getting
a really gnarly rootball or cross grained chunk. I
do, however, have a least favourite: ARBUTUS. I
think my success rate on that is about 15%!
What finishes do you prefer using?
My go-to finish is tung oil. I use an equal mix of
pure tung oil, polymerized tung oil and paint thinner. This seems to give me good penetration and
reasonable drying time even if it does take multiple
coats to give a good seal. My final finish is buffing
with Tripoli and carnauba wax. I have used epoxy
on some pieces but it never seems to be worth the
cost and effort.
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
I’ve dabbled with coloured epoxy, pewa’s, leather
and wire to accessorize cracks but only to avoid
throwing out a piece.
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
With my background, if it’s made out of wood, I’ve
probably done it at some point in my life. Full on
houses, far too many reno’s, furniture etc. I’ve had
three post retirement hobbies. The first was designing, building and flying remote control scale
sailplanes. Structure and control surface ratios are
rarely scalable so you have to get creative to both
look like the original but still be able to fly.
My second hobby was building small boats. Most
of these were cedar strip kayaks but there were
the occasional dinghy and pulling boats. Like the
gliders, the compromise was always weight vs
strength.
(Continued from page 9)
(Continued on page 11)
RC Sailplane

March 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
My third hobby (turning) came about in a strange
way. I was building a post and beam structure and
needed 120 tapered trunnels. As these were in the
“unobtainable” category, I bought a midi lathe and
made them. Then I met some turners and my life
changed again.
What inspires you - where do you get your
ideas from?
Like most of us, we follow what interests us. I get
ideas from friends, the guild, and more broadly,
the internet. But to inspire me, I need a challenge. How thin can I go on a voided root
ball? How deep can I make a vase?
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
The most admired turners that I have are David
Ellsworth and John Tisdale.
However, without a doubt, the most influence has
been my “Sensei” Rich Schmid. Without his guidance, encouragement and friendship, I would have
given up long ago.
Where do you usually display and/or sell your
work?
Because I live in a busy tourist area, I generally sell
from my house. While the walk in trade is good,
most of my volume are previous customers or
word of mouth. I have a terrible time at craft
shows as I’m anti-social by nature and hate the
pack up, set up, sit for 8 hours, pack up and unpack. Selling from my home allows me to work
when my studio is open and can demonstrate to
my customers that by being covered in sawdust, I
actually make the stuff.
What is the most challenging piece that you
have made so far?
It was a rootball for some friends that were moving
out of an old family home. They wanted a sentimental piece from an ornamental bush. They had
dug it out to take to their new home but after doing so, realized that it wasn’t going to live. I pressure washed as much soil and rock as it could, then
cut off the outlier roots. I was left with a somewhat solid 13” chunk. After rounding it, I started to
hollow and found that there was as much void as
there was wood. I strapped the outside with filament tape and kept going. In the end, I got the
(Continued from page 10)
(Continued on page 12)
Kayak Trio
Rootball

March 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
wall down to about 3/8” before my nerve gave
out. I never did get the inside very smooth but the
outside had lots of colour and character. They
loved it, which really made it worth it.
What is your favorite project to date?
Early on in my hollowing adventures, I copied one
of David Ellsworths creations. While the outside is
unremarkable, making the tools to hollow out to
the edges was both challenging and instructive. Well worth the effort.
Where do you see your work going in the future?
Absolutely no idea. What ever whim tickles my
fancy!

From Dale Larson, AAW Symposium Chair, please
send out to membership
We had an AAW symposium committee meeting
Feb 20th. We are three months from the symposium here in Portland. The registration numbers are
looking very good. There should be a good turnout. There are a great bunch of demonstrators and
variety of topics being covered. The demonstration
schedule is done and is being polished up. It
should be posted on the AAW website shortly. I
know some members have been waiting to look at
the schedule before committing where to volunteer during the symposium. I know from past symposiums it simply takes a lot of volunteer help to
make the symposium a success. If everyone helps
a little, the work gets done.
Signing up to volunteer is easy. Go to the AAW
website https://www.woodturner.org/ and click on
the symposium logo. Then scroll down and click on
volunteer, then "Sign Up" . It will take you to Sign
Up Genius where all the committees are listed. See
where you are interested and sign up.
There are a couple of areas we could use some
help on. Videographers. This is the one area of volunteer help that comes with a free registration. If
you have experience as a videographer and are interested
contact
Tom
Lawson
at
morningstar_family@yahoo.com. Tom is the national
lead on videographers and Steve Walgrave is the
local lead.
The Youth turning room is a great place to help
young turners get some time on the lathe. It takes
a lot of hands to help on each lathe. The reward is
that it brings a big smile to these young faces. Larry Curry is the local lead. You can go directly to
Sign Up Genius or contact Larry at lgcurry@aol.com.
If your spouse will be at the symposium we have a
couple of areas that they can help with if they like
keeping busy. If your spouse is craft oriented, we
have a space for spouses to meet and work on craft
projects. They can help organize projects or just be
a good host to out of town spouses. The AAW
merchandise booth sells AAW tshirts, books and
the like. We could use some help there.
From personal experience I can tell you that volunteering at the AAW symposiums over the past 17
years has changed my life. I now have friends all
over the country and around the world. Volunteering brings you into contact with some wonderful
and talented turners. You will develop life long
friends. And these contacts can pay off for your
chapter. You find out which demonstrators like to
travel and it gives you a chance to ask them to
come to your chapter.
If you have any questions feel free to contact me at
woodbowl@frontier.com
Dale Larson

March 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
As crazy busy as things have been, I shockingly
etched out a bunch of time this past month for
making. Have I mentioned how much I love to
make shavings? I find it so energizing and that I get
gleeful and giddy as the ribbons peel off or the fine
cuts delightfully curl, as the form takes shape.
There are simply so many things about the endeavour of woodturning that I find delightful and as my
journey into this activity evolves, I am noticing
some shifts.
My wood supply has seen a massive upgrade this
month. So much so that this spring when we get a
consistent period of sun, I absolutely need to find
some time to pile the horde of wood into a space
and pick through what stays and what gets gifted
to my neighbours as firewood. Since before becoming a woodturner I started collecting wood for
possible projects and every chance I got I clamoured for another chunk of wood…especially if it
was pretty, (aka spalted or burl), holly, boxwood,
amboyna or something I had yet to turn.
I’ll even chase cherry. So, when
a long-time friend called and
asked if I wanted some cherry
for turning, of course I said yes,
and my day completely shifted
from what I was going to do.
Within the hour I was in his car,
loaded with chainsaws and
gear, we drove to a location
nearby to harvest a tree that
recently came down. Turns
out, we drove to a home of
friends I had while the kids were in school…lovely
couple…perhaps some of my favourite people from
that era of time. It did not take us long to make
some cuts, load his car and require more fuel and a
sharpening. While Rick serviced his saw, I unloaded and squirrelled away the stash…trying to pick
spots out of the sun and to hide it from family’s
eyes…as they are already on my case for having
way too much wood. But we still went back for a
second load and sadly, left a bunch behind.
But as the conversation happened at
the February GVWG
meeting, I knew I
had to get to this
wood ASAP, or it
would be lost to
cracks and would
simply become a
pile of firewood. One way to process the wood
was to share it. So, wherever I went and whomever I met with, they got some chunks of cherry (if
they wanted it… a few did decline…figure they are
more disciplined with their wood supply than I am).
I also processed a bunch of the wood to become
bowl blanks of a smaller size so I could handle
them on my smaller lathe. So this is why I keep
hearing from the seasoned turners you must have
a band saw…or friends who will let you use theirs?
I had tried to make a bunch of smaller pieces as I
know Rick really has the desire to turn a bowl. He
did so long ago while on a vacation in Hawaii and
he caught the bug…but his life is still too busy to
get himself behind a lathe…but when he does, I
know he will be great at turning a bowl. He was
hoping to come to our meetings, but currently he
has another long-standing commitment that is on
Thursday evenings, so he isn’t going to scratch that
itch just yet.
But I did. And because I
saw Keith Ruttan’s gorgeous results with pretty
wood, I asked if I could
come and pick through
the corners that he cut off
to make his bowls. That
resulted in yet another
car full of wood, so ready
for the lathe as it is, but a
(Continued on page 14)

bunch that had to get processed. Which meant
another day hanging out with another turner making lots of cuts on a band saw. Oh, the wood! It
mostly is intended to become pen blanks, but there
were some pretty curly maple chunks, one which
became a candle holder. This project is still a work
in progress as I got an idea from Gary Burns and
from my collection that I have yet to execute. But
funnily enough, some of the pieces decided to become tiny dishes and not pen blanks at all.
The small pieces I will happily turn
on my lathe, even loving the interrupted cuts necessary to make it
round. If the piece started out
square, it would have likely become a square platter, but instead
it became a lovely little dish. The wife of another
turner delightfully exclaimed it would be perfect on
a bedside table to place earrings in. Absolutely!
But what I also concluded
this month, even though I
had trimmed corners and
make the wood better balanced, some of these cherry
chunks were still too big to
turn on my little lathe. So
back to a friends’ house who
has a bigger lathe and bigger
bowl gouges that he would
let me use. For two full days
he let me come and play. At
one point, for one of the chunks of wood that was
brutal on the tools, he was sharpening one gouge
while I used the other to turn. By the time he got it
sharp, I handed the tool I was using when taking
the fresh tool. It didn’t take long before he insisted, I sharpen the tools myself. Here was a living
example of why having a sharpening system that
allows you to replicate the grind is absolutely essential to your wood shop. Except for one time
that I failed to get the wolverine jig set up in the
correct place, I was easily able to replicate the
grind of his gouges. And sharp tools make all the
difference for the task of turning this wood.
And given the larger lathe, and the IRD by Paul Russel, of course I took some pieces
and made them into something
inspired by Paul’s Barley There

their stories, talking through the choices and considerations, being encouraged to take my work
even further, my skill level has
seen an exponential growth
this past month. AND my energy level to handle the other
stuff in my life has become
much improved. I find it easier
to do the necessary and mundane following the release of
endorphins that I get when I
turn, especially when I connect
and turn with others.

my students music in the evenings. How amazing
might that be? A trifecta of activity that would
charge me up one day a week. Surely, I would

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 37)

March 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 37
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
